one_line: Jellyfish data from ~50k engineers: switching AI models or tools barely moves merged PRs, while skill use, token volume, company and individual engineer effects explain far more.
summary: Nicholas Arcolano (head of AI and research at Jellyfish) argues that if AI isn't producing the outcomes you want, the cause is usually the team and the engineer, not the model. He opens with a natural experiment: a Cursor UI change pushed Grok usage sharply upward, and per-engineer merged PRs showed no statistical relationship with the shift. He then uses a curated dataset (about 50,000 engineers at 447 companies, Cursor and Claude Code users) to split the variation in merged PRs per engineer per week into components. Tool and model switches explain under 1%, skill use about 3% (with a large effect at high usage), token consumption about 9%, and company or team about 12%, leaving roughly three quarters for the individual engineer. Token spend shows diminishing returns, and the spread between top and bottom engineers and companies is wide even at fixed consumption. A small longitudinal check found top-quartile engineers churn about as much after AI adoption as before, so he sees no large reshuffling of who is productive. His closing advice is that leaders control the people and organization levers, not the tools.

key_ideas.idea: Poor AI outcomes are more likely a team and process problem than a model problem.
key_ideas.detail: The talk frames the model as the 'clubs' in a golf analogy: the outcome depends mainly on how the engineer and organization use it.

key_ideas.idea: A natural experiment found no output change when engineers were pushed toward Grok.
key_ideas.detail: A Cursor UI and auto-mode change drove a large, fast shift to Grok. Per-engineer change in merged PRs, relative to same-company colleagues, showed no statistical correlation with the shift in model share. The speaker says this is an external shock, so it is a useful causal test.

key_ideas.idea: Output is decomposed into tool, skill use, consumption, company or team, and individual factors.
key_ideas.detail: Using a statistical model on merged PRs per engineer per week, the speaker reports the tool at under 1%, skill use at about 3%, token consumption at about 9%, where you work at about 12%, and the individual as the largest piece (about three quarters of the model).

key_ideas.idea: Switching tools, models or harnesses has little measurable effect on throughput.
key_ideas.detail: Engineers compared with themselves moved between Opus and Sonnet, ChatGPT, Cursor and Claude Code, and autocomplete to agentic mode. The speaker calls the effect statistically a nothing burger.

key_ideas.idea: Skill use matters more than model choice, but most engineers barely use skills.
key_ideas.detail: As of September, almost half of engineer-weeks had essentially zero skill use, and only 12% were at a level the speaker considers modern AI engineering practice. At 30 or more skill runs per engineer per week, the speaker reports about a 30% throughput bump, holding other factors constant.

Across about 500,000 developer-weeks, more tokens gave more merged PRs on a saturating curve, which the speaker likens to a rocket equation. The top 10% versus the median roughly doubles output for about 10x the tokens.

key_ideas.idea: Company and team effects are large even at fixed AI spend.
key_ideas.detail: Of the company-level factor, about one third is team and two thirds is company (codebase, review process, culture). Holding consumption fixed, the top-10% companies produce about 2x the output of the bottom-10% companies.

key_ideas.idea: Individual variation is the biggest lever, and AI is not reshuffling the top engineers.
key_ideas.detail: The bottom-to-top-10% spread among engineers is about 3.5x, wider than the company spread. In a small longitudinal study of about 10,000 engineers, about 44% dropped out of the top productivity quartile each half-year before AI and about 41% after.

techniques.name: Natural experiment from a vendor-driven shock
techniques.how: When a tool vendor changes its UI or defaults (e.g. promoting a model in auto mode), treat the resulting shift in per-user model share as exogenous. For each engineer, compute the change in merged PRs per week relative to same-company colleagues, then plot it against the change in share of usage on the new model. Use a near-zero correlation as evidence the model did not drive output.
techniques.when: When you want a causal read on a tool or model change without running an A/B test, and you have per-user telemetry plus a clear external shock.

techniques.name: Within-engineer switch comparison
techniques.how: Compare each engineer's output before and after a change in their own behavior (model switch, harness switch, autocomplete to agentic mode), so each person serves as their own baseline.
techniques.when: When evaluating a tool migration or rollout and you want to control for individual skill.

techniques.name: Variance decomposition of throughput
techniques.how: Fit a statistical model of the outcome (merged PRs per engineer per week) with factor groups: tool, skill use, consumption (tokens or active days), company or team (environment), and individual. Report each group's share of explained variance, holding the others constant.
techniques.when: When you need to tell leadership where to spend effort: the tool, the usage habits, or the org and people. The talk's argument rests on this breakdown.

techniques.name: Skill-use level bins over time
techniques.how: Classify each engineer-week into zero, low, medium or high skill use (by number of skill runs), then track the share of weeks in each bin over time to see adoption depth, not just whether skills are installed.
techniques.when: When measuring how well a team uses agent skills or harness customization, as opposed to whether the feature exists.

techniques.name: Percentile binning of consumption against output
techniques.how: Group developer-weeks into percentile bins by token spend, plot average tokens against average merged PRs per week for each bin, then fit a saturating curve. Compare the top 10% with the median to estimate the return on extra tokens.
techniques.when: When deciding how much token budget to give engineers and whether more spend is likely to pay off.

techniques.name: Longitudinal rank-stability check
techniques.how: Rank engineers by output each quarter or half-year, measure how many leave the top quartile each period, and compare the rate before and after a change such as AI adoption. A stable rate suggests the rank order did not change.
techniques.when: When testing the claim that a new technology levels the playing field or reshuffles who is productive.

numbers.claim: Dataset for the model-switching analysis: about 50,000 engineers at 447 companies, Cursor and Claude Code users, merged PRs per engineer per week as the output metric.
Tool or model switching explains under 1% of variation in merged PRs per engineer per week.
Skill use explains about 3% of variation. As of September, almost half of engineer-weeks had zero skill use and 12% were at a high level.
Token consumption explains about 9% of variation. Based on about 500,000 developer-weeks, the top 10% produce about 2x the merged PRs of the median at about 10x the tokens.
Company or team (where you work) explains about 12% of variation. Of that factor, about one third is team and two thirds is company.
Individual engineer is about three quarters of the statistical model (the speaker's stated share).
Holding consumption fixed, the top-10% companies produce about 2x the merged PRs of the bottom-10% companies.
At 30 or more skill runs per engineer per week, the speaker reports about a 30% throughput bump, holding other factors constant.
The spread from the bottom 10% to the top 10% of engineers is about 3.5x, versus about 2x for companies.
In a longitudinal study of about 10,000 engineers, about 44% leave the top productivity quartile every half-year before AI and about 41% after.

hot_takes: Vendor data with a pitch: Jellyfish sells engineering analytics, and the closing plugs its monthly benchmarks and Substack. The dataset is large but proprietary and not reproducible from the talk.

The 'no effect of model' result comes from one natural experiment and a correlational regression. The speaker says there is no quality metric in the analysis and that the model was not tested on quality.

The variance shares are stated only loosely. Tool (under 1%), skills (3%), consumption (9%) and company (12%) sum to about 25%, which matches the speaker's claim that the individual is about three quarters, but the talk does not say whether these are shares of explained variance or of total variance. Method details are skipped.

The Grok shift is attributed to Cursor's UI and auto-mode changes, and the speaker says it followed an acquisition announcement (he said SpaceX and Cursor). The transcript only supports the speaker's own account of those events.

The 'AI does not reshuffle the top engineers' finding comes from a small quarterly-rank churn study, with the before and after numbers (44% and 41%) very close. The speaker doesn't give significance tests here.

relevance.why: SkillForge is meant to mine agent telemetry into reusable skills, and this talk's finding that skill-use depth matters more than model choice is a concrete signal for that work. The talk does not address the open question of how to score skill-worthiness.
relevance.action: Add a skill-use depth metric (zero, low, medium, high by runs per engineer-week) to SkillForge's telemetry analysis and track its trend as a success signal.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps Claude Code, and the talk finds skill use and harness customization matter more than the model. The data is about adoption, not harness design, so the link is indirect.
relevance.action: Log skill invocations per run in ProsHarness and check whether high-skill runs produce better checkpointed outcomes before ranking skills.
